ito-guide--communications-antenna.mu.content:
>Positioning a radio antenna
A clear, safely positioned antenna can improve a link; test both directions.

Keep antennas upright if that is how they are designed and the other station is similarly polarised. An unobstructed position, or greater safe height, may help reduce the effect of buildings and terrain. Trees and wet materials can also weaken a signal. Move a portable radio a short distance and test again.
Keep antenna cables as short as practical and use suitable connectors. Turn the transmitter off before disconnecting an antenna. Never install an antenna near overhead power lines; do not climb a roof or tree during bad weather. Use qualified help for permanent outdoor installations, earthing and lightning protection.
Antenna gain and cable loss affect radiated power. Make sure the complete installation meets the applicable legal limits.

ito-guide--communications-emergency.mu.content:
>Getting emergency help
For immediate danger call 999 or 112 and ask for the emergency service you need.

Give your location, what happened, people involved and a number for a return call. Follow the call handler’s instructions. In the hills or mountains ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue; at the coast ask for Coastguard.
A mobile 999 or 112 call can use another available UK network if your own has no coverage. Some phones offer emergency satellite contact where supported; it depends on the device, service and conditions. Emergency SMS requires registration in advance: text register to 999 and follow the reply. It still needs a mobile network.
A Reticulum or LoRa message does not directly reach 999 unless a specific service has confirmed it can receive and relay it. Do not assume anyone is monitoring.

ito-guide--communications-licensing.mu.content:
>UK radio rules
Before transmitting, check the conditions that apply to your exact equipment, frequency and use.

Licence-exempt does not mean unrestricted. UK short-range radio rules can specify frequency ranges, radiated power, antenna and airtime limits. Conditions vary by sub-band and may change. Check current Ofcom requirements and the equipment instructions; transmitter power alone is not the same as radiated power.
PMR446 handheld radios have their own equipment and use rules. Shared channels are not private or protected from interference. An amateur radio licence has separate conditions; do not assume it authorises encrypted Reticulum traffic. Ofcom’s amateur guidance restricts encrypted messages between amateur stations, with specified exceptions.
This page is a starting point, not a full licence. Follow the relevant current licence or exemption for your installation.

ito-guide--communications-location.mu.content:
>Communicating your location
Write a position that can be read back without your map or phone.
1. Start with a grid reference or latitude and longitude. State the system. Give coordinates in the order shown by the device, with hemisphere or signed values and any uncertainty. Never silently convert formats under pressure.
2. Add a landmark, route, direction and estimated distance from the landmark. Say whether you are staying there and how rescuers might approach.
3. Give the incident, group count, immediate hazards and callback number. Ask the recipient to repeat the position. Correct mismatches before ending contact.
4. If you have no fix, give the last confirmed point, direction and elapsed travel time. Avoid presenting estimated coordinates as exact.

ito-guide--communications-lora.mu.content:
>LoRa basics
LoRa is a low-power radio method; compatible settings and software are needed at both ends.

LoRa can carry small amounts of data over long distances in suitable conditions, but buildings, terrain, trees, interference and antenna placement change the result. Radio bandwidth, spreading factor and coding rate affect range and speed. Both ends of a direct link must use compatible radio settings and the same network protocol.
Reticulum can use compatible RNode radios. LoRa alone does not mean that a device supports Reticulum, MeshCore, Meshtastic or LoRaWAN interchangeably. A page transfer can take a long time or fail, especially across several hops.
Shared frequencies have legal operating limits. Do not assume higher power or a larger antenna is permitted.

ito-guide--communications-mesh.mu.content:
>How network relays work
A relay can extend reach only if it is compatible, powered and able to hear both sides.

In a multi-hop network, information may pass through intermediate nodes. Reticulum transport must be enabled on nodes intended to forward traffic. A node within radio range is not automatically a usable relay; settings, paths and network load matter.
Each radio hop uses shared airtime. Weak links, interference or a powered-off relay can delay or stop delivery. A stronger signal from one neighbour does not prove the full path or return path works.
Test messages both ways with a known person before relying on a route. Keep messages short and do not repeatedly flood the channel with retries.

ito-guide--communications-morse.mu.content:
>Morse timing and the SOS signal
Use distinct short and long pulses that can be recognised at a distance.
1. Choose a unit of time you can repeat. A dot lasts one unit and a dash three. Pause one unit between elements of a character, three between ordinary characters and seven between words.
2. SOS is sent as a single distress sequence: three short, three long, three short, with short element gaps throughout. Pause between repeats to listen or look for a reply.
3. Practise with a switched torch from a safe position. In a real emergency use the recognised local signal where known. UK hill teams advise six flashes or whistle blasts followed by a one-minute pause.
4. Treat the signal as a way to attract attention. Keep trying confirmed emergency routes rather than assuming someone saw it.

ito-guide--communications-nomad.mu.content:
>Nomad Network basics
Nomad Network lets a node host small pages that other reachable nodes can read.

A host must be powered, have hosting enabled and be reachable over Reticulum. Use the host’s Nomad destination address in a compatible browser. Pages can link to others on the same host or another destination; another host may not be reachable.
Choose short text pages on slow radio. A page that was cached on your device may be available offline, depending on the client and its cache settings; test this before relying on it. A node may be offline, pages may be old, and a destination address does not certify the accuracy of content.
Ito support is under development. The steps and availability in a finished Ito interface have not yet been verified.

ito-guide--communications-offline.mu.content:
>Communicating without internet
Agree a primary and backup method with people before an outage.

A direct radio or local Reticulum path can work without internet if all required devices, compatible links and power are available. A route that normally uses an internet-connected relay will fail if that connection is lost and no other route is available.
Keep written phone numbers, agreed radio settings and destination addresses. Test in both directions with the internet disconnected. Agree check-in times and a meeting place. A battery radio can receive public broadcasts if a local station is operating, but reception is not two-way communication.
For an emergency try 999 or 112 first. A mesh message is not a confirmed emergency-service call; seek another route to help if no acknowledgement arrives.

ito-guide--communications-planning.mu.content:
>Practising an emergency communications plan
Agree who listens, when they listen and what they do after silence.
1. Write the primary contact route and two alternatives on a card. Include contact names, devices and the agreed channel or address. Confirm that all participants can use the equipment lawfully.
2. Agree check-in times, locations and how long to wait before taking action. Choose a safe meeting point and nominate who will contact emergency services if a person is overdue.
3. Practise from the actual locations. Check that messages can be received and read back. Simulate loss of mobile data without transmitting a false distress call.
4. Record dead spots and revise the fallback route. Leave a copy with someone outside the group. When the plan changes, tell everyone affected.

ito-guide--communications-power.mu.content:
>Making radio batteries last
Schedule transmissions while keeping an agreed way to receive replies.
1. Charge devices before departure. Mark each battery as charged or used and carry protected spares. Check connectors and power settings with the equipment manual.
2. Disable unused radios or displays where this does not prevent contact. Use scheduled check-ins only when all parties know the schedule. Keep a rescue callback device on if rescuers expect to call.
3. Keep batteries dry and within their stated temperature limits. Protect loose terminals from metal. Use a compatible cable and charger.
4. After a missed check-in, use the agreed fallback rather than draining batteries with continuous calls. Preserve a separate reserve for distress or navigation.

ito-guide--communications-radio.mu.content:
>Passing an emergency message by radio
Write the message before transmitting and verify that someone received it.
1. Use authorised equipment and the agreed channel. Listen first. If calling a known contact, name them and identify yourself. On a shared channel, transmit only information needed for help.
2. Press transmit, wait briefly, then state location and format, incident, number of people, immediate dangers and help needed. Release the button and listen.
3. Ask for a readback of the location and confirmation of who will call rescue. If no reply, retry from a safe position or use the agreed fallback route.
4. Keep a written message and time for relays. A radio, LoRa or Reticulum transmission does not confirm anyone is monitoring. Use direct emergency services whenever available.

ito-guide--communications-reticulum.mu.content:
>Reticulum basics
Reticulum is a networking system that can operate over several kinds of connection.

Devices use destinations to address services or people. Nodes announce destinations and, where configured as transport nodes, can forward traffic over available interfaces. A path may include more than one hop. Reticulum can use radio, local networks or internet links; a route is not guaranteed to exist.
Links encrypt data between endpoints, but this does not prove that the person or information at the other end is trustworthy. Verify identities and destination addresses in advance. Keep a backup of your identity using the application’s instructions and protect it from others.
An internet outage does not disable a purely local radio path, but devices, power, compatible settings and a reachable peer are still needed.

ito-guide--communications-signal.mu.content:
>Understanding radio signal
A received signal reading is a clue, not a delivery guarantee.

RSSI describes received signal strength, commonly in dBm: a value closer to zero is stronger, so -90 dBm is stronger than -110 dBm. SNR compares signal with noise; a larger value generally means more margin above noise. Some LoRa signals can be decoded at negative SNR, depending on settings and conditions.
Readings usually describe what your device received, not what the other person received. Different transmit power, antennas, obstructions and interference can make the two directions perform differently. Multi-hop readings may describe only part of the route.
Compare repeated tests with the same settings and a known peer. A successful reply or delivery acknowledgement is more useful than a single signal reading.

ito-guide--communications-visual.mu.content:
>Making a visible rescue signal
Use contrast by day and a controlled light signal at night.
1. From safe ground, look at your position from the likely rescue approach. Choose an open patch with strong contrast, such as a bright cloth against dark soil. Secure it flat against wind.
2. If you see rescuers, wave a bright garment where you can be seen without approaching cliffs, flowing water or traffic. Keep visual contact from a safe position.
3. At night use a torch in the local distress pattern. Keep a second light or spare battery for movement and care. Avoid lasers, flares or smoke as improvised signals.
4. If you must move to escape danger, communicate your new position as soon as possible. A marker alone cannot tell a rescue party where you went.

ito-guide--fire-control.mu.content:
>Maintaining a small cooking fire
Maintain controllable heat for a pot rather than building a large flame.
1. Use an existing approved grate or stable cooking support. Test the cold setup with a filled pot before lighting. Keep handles where they cannot be knocked or touched accidentally.
2. Add small amounts of dry fuel and allow manageable embers to form. Keep air gaps and move the pot only if you can do so with dry heat-resistant gloves.
3. Use a lid and heat only the water needed. Remove the pan if flames flare around it; if lifting it is unsafe, step back and allow the fire to settle. Keep children and pets away.
4. Stop feeding the fire early enough to extinguish it fully. Stay until the remains are cold.

ito-guide--fire-fuel.mu.content:
>Selecting and sorting firewood
Use approved supplied fuel first. Gather small dead fallen wood only where permitted.
1. Sort by thickness before lighting. Look for pieces that snap cleanly rather than bending. Wet bark can conceal drier wood, but heavy damp fuel will smoulder and make smoke.
2. Reject painted, treated or glued timber, plastics and unknown scrap. Leave habitat wood, standing dead trees and living vegetation in place. Never bring unknown firewood into areas with pest restrictions.
3. Keep enough small pieces for the task and avoid a surplus on the fire. Keep the reserve out of the spark area and off damp ground.
4. If the fire begins smoking heavily or fuel will not burn cleanly, stop adding wood. Let the small fire burn down under supervision and extinguish it.

ito-guide--fire-matches.mu.content:
>Lighting with matches or a lighter
Light only a small prepared fire at a permitted site.
1. Place ready tinder, fine kindling and water beside the designated fire area. Shelter the match with your hands or body from a light breeze while staying clear of the tinder's smoke path. Cancel in strong wind.
2. Hold the flame to the edge of the tinder, let it establish, and add a few thin pieces with air gaps. Wait for those pieces to catch before adding the next size.
3. Extinguish each spent match completely and keep it in the fire area until cold. Keep matches and the lighter away from heat, children and wet ground.
4. If the fire repeatedly dies, correct damp fuel or poor airflow. Never pour petrol or another accelerant into the fire or onto warm material.

ito-guide--fire-put-out.mu.content:
>Extinguishing a campfire
Leave enough water and time to cool every ember.
1. Stop adding wood well before departure. When it is safe to approach, carefully wet the fire remains. Beware hot steam and ash. Stir with a tool to uncover hidden embers and wet them again.
2. Continue adding water and stirring until the remains and edges are cold throughout. Check for heat without putting your bare hand in the ash. Recheck for smoke, glowing material or warmth before leaving.
3. Do not bury hot remains or assume a layer of sand, rain or darkness means the fire is out. Subsurface fuel can stay hot. Follow site rules for cold ash disposal.
4. If fire spreads beyond the ring or you cannot control it safely, leave the area, alert others and call the local emergency number when reachable.

ito-guide--fire-setup.mu.content:
>Preparing a small outdoor fire
Plan the entire burn, including putting it out, before lighting.
1. Decide whether you need flame at all. Dry layers, a cold meal or a lawful outdoor stove may solve the problem. Check permission, weather and the site's fire facilities before gathering anything.
2. Reserve enough water to extinguish the fire. Set out a stirring tool. Put a small dry tinder bundle, fine kindling and slightly larger fuel in separate groups. Keep spare fuel outside the spark area.
3. Think in terms of heat, fuel and oxygen. A few fine pieces catch before thicker pieces can. Leave air gaps and feed small amounts only when the previous pieces are alight. If smoke rises but flame disappears, check for damp fuel or an overloaded pile.
4. Assign someone to stay until extinguishing is complete. If you cannot keep the burn small or stop it safely, leave it unlit.

ito-guide--fire-site.mu.content:
>Choosing a safe fire site
Use a fire only where you have permission, conditions are suitable and you can extinguish it.
1. Check restrictions and campsite rules. In dry or gusty weather, or if you cannot find out whether fires are allowed, use cold food or another lawful, safer option.
2. Prefer the site's designated fire ring or approved facility. Keep clear of tents, buildings, branches, roots, dry vegetation and peat. A thin layer of soil can hide roots or organic material that will smoulder.
3. Work outdoors in open air, never under a tarp or in a tent. Check wind direction and where sparks could land. Set water and a stirring tool within reach, and keep a clear way out.
4. Cancel if wind increases, ash blows beyond the site, or you cannot reserve enough water to extinguish and cool everything.

ito-guide--fire-spark.mu.content:
>Using a ferrocerium rod
Practise spark ignition at a permitted fire site with water ready.
1. Use the rod's designated scraper and a small nest of dry, fine tinder. Set the nest inside the fire area. Collect kindling in advance so you do not leave a developing flame alone.
2. Place the rod tip close to the tinder. Keep the scraper steady near the tinder and draw the rod back so sparks land on the material without scattering it.
3. When tinder catches, add fine dry kindling a little at a time, leaving airflow. Do not use powder from unknown sources or liquid fuel to help it catch.
4. If sparks bounce off, dry or tease apart the tinder and try again only while conditions are safe. Stop if sparks are blowing outside the designated area.

ito-guide--fire-tinder.mu.content:
>Preparing tinder and kindling
Prepare all fuel sizes before striking a match at a permitted site.
1. Keep a small dry tinder supply in a sealed bag. Use plain dry paper or a purpose-made firelighter according to its directions. Where collecting is allowed, finely split dry woody material can supplement it.
2. Lay out fine dry pieces, pencil-sized kindling and slightly thicker pieces separately. Use small readily controlled fuel that can burn down completely.
3. Arrange tinder where air can reach it. Put only a few fine pieces above it at first, leaving an opening for ignition. Keep spare fuel beyond reach of sparks.
4. If the tinder blackens without catching, check dampness and airflow. Replace damp material rather than adding liquid fuel, aerosols or treated scraps. Abort if no dry supply is available.

ito-guide--fire-wet.mu.content:
>Cooking heat in wet weather
Choose a cold meal first if you cannot maintain safe heat outdoors.
1. Keep ignition supplies in a waterproof pouch. Check that the authorised fire site is usable and that wind will not carry embers. Never move a flame under your shelter to keep it dry.
2. Set tinder and dry kindling aside before exposing a batch to rain. If allowed, use the dry interior of small split sticks or take fuel from your protected supply. Keep wet wood off the initial fire.
3. Start with the smallest flame needed and add dry wood slowly. If the fire will not hold without large amounts of fuel, abandon it and extinguish it fully. Wet ground and rain can leave buried embers alive.

ito-guide--first-aid-adult-cpr.mu.content:
>Adult CPR and defibrillator
Unresponsive and not breathing normally, or only gasping: call 999 and start CPR.

1. Put the phone on speaker. Ask someone to bring an AED (defibrillator) if available; do not leave the person to fetch one if alone.
2. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top. With straight arms, push down 5 to 6 cm, 100 to 120 times a minute. Let the chest rise fully after each push.
3. Continue compressions. If trained and willing to give breaths, use 30 compressions then 2 breaths. Follow the call handler’s instructions.
4. Switch on the AED as soon as it arrives, attach pads to the bare chest and follow its voice prompts. Keep clear when told; resume CPR when instructed.
Continue until the person shows signs of life or a professional takes over. Child and baby CPR differs: see Child CPR.

ito-guide--first-aid-assess.mu.content:
>Assessing an emergency
Treat threats to life before making a detailed assessment.
1. Stop and look for traffic, electricity, fire, unstable ground or moving water. Do not approach through danger. Ask a helper to make the area safe if they can.
2. Check responsiveness by speaking loudly and gently touching the shoulders. Look for life-threatening bleeding and put direct pressure on it or ask a helper to do so.
3. If unresponsive, call emergency services immediately (UK: 999 or 112), preferably on speaker. Open the airway and check breathing while the call connects. Gasping or slow irregular breaths are abnormal. Start CPR if breathing is abnormal or absent and fetch an AED if available.
4. If breathing normally, maintain the airway and follow dispatch advice. Keep checking breathing and response. If trauma is suspected, minimise movement unless necessary for safety, breathing or immediate care.

ito-guide--first-aid-bleeding.mu.content:
>Controlling severe bleeding
Apply direct pressure immediately and get help.
1. Use gloves if ready, but do not delay. Press hard directly on the wound with a dressing, clean cloth or hand if needed. Tell a helper to call emergency services and fetch a first-aid kit.
2. If an object is embedded, leave it in place. Press to either side of the object without pushing it deeper. Keep pressure continuous.
3. For life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure fails to stop, a commercial tourniquet may be needed. Use one if trained or guided by emergency dispatch. Note the application time and do not release it yourself.
4. Keep the person warm and watch breathing and response. If they are unresponsive and breathing abnormally, begin CPR. Hand over what happened, when it happened and what you did.

ito-guide--first-aid-burns.mu.content:
>Cooling and covering burns
Stop the burning and cool the affected skin as soon as possible.
1. Move the person away from the heat when safe. For electrical contact, isolate the supply before touching them. Remove nearby jewellery and clothing before swelling, leaving anything stuck to the skin in place.
2. Cool under cool running water. Aim for 20 minutes where possible. Keep the rest of the person warm, particularly children or anyone with extensive burns. Avoid ice, creams and grease.
3. After cooling, lay clean cling film loosely over the burn if suitable, without wrapping a limb or covering the face. A clean non-fluffy dressing is an alternative. Leave blisters intact.
4. Get urgent help for large, deep, electrical or chemical burns, or breathing difficulty after smoke exposure. Seek medical advice for significant burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals or major joints.

ito-guide--first-aid-child-cpr.mu.content:
>Child and baby CPR
A child or baby who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs immediate CPR.

Call 999 on speaker and follow the call handler. Gasping is not normal breathing. If possible have someone bring an AED without delaying CPR.
Open the airway and give 5 initial rescue breaths, each about one second, looking for the chest to rise. For a baby, cover both mouth and nose with your mouth. Then give 30 chest compressions followed by 2 breaths, repeating. Push in the centre of the chest to about one third of its depth; use one or two hands for a child, or the two-thumb encircling technique for an infant.
If unable or unwilling to give breaths, give chest compressions. Apply the AED as soon as available; use child pads or child mode if available without delaying treatment. Follow prompts. Continue until help takes over or the child shows signs of life.

ito-guide--first-aid-choking-baby.mu.content:
>Choking: baby under one
Call 999 on speaker and act immediately if the baby cannot cough, cry or breathe effectively.

1. Support the head and place the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than the chest. Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades.
2. If still choking, turn the baby face up on your knees, supporting the head. Give up to 5 sharp chest thrusts in the centre of the chest, using the two-thumb encircling technique.
3. Alternate up to 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts. Stop as soon as the obstruction clears. Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby. Do not sweep blindly inside the mouth; remove an object only if clearly visible.
If the baby becomes unresponsive, start child and baby CPR, beginning with 5 rescue breaths. Follow the call handler. Seek a healthcare assessment after chest thrusts.

ito-guide--first-aid-choking.mu.content:
>Choking: adults and children
Call 999 as soon as you recognise choking; use speaker if alone.

If they can cough effectively, encourage coughing. If they cannot cough effectively, speak or breathe, act immediately.
For adults and children over one: lean them forwards and give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades. If still choking, stand behind, place a fist between the navel and bottom of the breastbone, grasp it and pull sharply inwards and upwards up to 5 times. Alternate 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until clear or unresponsive.
For a pregnant person, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Do not use abdominal thrusts on a baby under one: see Choking baby.
If unresponsive, start CPR. Only remove an object if clearly visible; never sweep blindly. After abdominal or chest thrusts, seek healthcare assessment, even if the person seems well.

Shelter gently. Remove wet clothing once sheltered and wrap in dry layers. Insulate from the ground. Stay and monitor breathing.

ito-guide--first-aid-evacuation.mu.content:
>Deciding whether to move a casualty
Weigh immediate danger against the risk of moving an injured person.
1. Move only as needed to escape immediate danger or deliver lifesaving care. Otherwise keep the casualty sheltered and still, particularly after a major fall or suspected spinal, pelvic or leg injury.
2. Call for rescue when possible. Share location, suspected injuries, breathing, responsiveness, dangers on approach and whether you can stay in place.
3. If you have no signal, use a prearranged relay or send a capable helper to a known safe contact point when doing so leaves adequate care with the casualty. Give them the location in writing and agree where to return.
4. Avoid improvised carries over treacherous terrain. If evacuation is unavoidable, reassess hazards, direction, group capacity and casualty condition before moving. Update rescuers if your location changes.

ito-guide--first-aid-fractures.mu.content:
>Supporting a suspected fracture
Support the injured part in the position found and avoid further movement.
1. Control serious bleeding first. For an open fracture cover the wound with a clean dressing and press to control bleeding around it, avoiding pressure on exposed bone.
2. Ask the person to keep still. Support the injury with hands or padding such as folded clothes. Do not straighten a deformed limb or push bone back in.
3. Note any numbness, tingling, unusual coldness or colour change below the injury and report it. Remove constricting jewellery if easily done without moving the injured part.
4. Get medical help. Avoid moving someone with a suspected spine, pelvis or upper-leg injury unless danger, airway care or resuscitation requires it. Keep them warm and reassess while waiting.

ito-guide--first-aid-heat.mu.content:
>Recognising and treating heat illness
Confusion, collapse or seizures in the heat can mean heatstroke.
1. Stop activity, move to shade or a cooler place, and remove excess clothing. For a fully alert person with suspected heat exhaustion, offer cool water or a rehydration drink and cool the skin with water and fanning.
2. If there is confusion, collapse, seizure, very high temperature or no improvement after 30 minutes of cooling, call emergency services. Start active cooling immediately; do not wait for transport.
3. Wet the skin with cool water and fan it. Continue cooling and monitor breathing. Do not give drinks if alertness or swallowing is impaired.
4. If unresponsive and breathing abnormally, start CPR and follow dispatch instructions. Share the timing of exposure, symptoms and cooling.

ito-guide--first-aid-hypothermia.mu.content:
>Hypothermia first aid
Treat confusion, drowsiness or slurred speech after cold exposure as urgent.
1. Call for emergency help. Handle the person gently and get them out of wind or rain when safe. Do not make a confused or exhausted casualty walk to warm up.
2. Insulate from the ground. Once sheltered, replace wet layers with dry ones and cover the head while keeping the face clear. Add a windproof layer and stay with the person.
3. Offer a warm non-alcoholic drink and sugary food only if fully awake and swallowing safely. Avoid alcohol, rubbing limbs and direct heat such as a hot bath or hot-water bottle.
4. Monitor response and breathing. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and follow dispatch instructions if reachable. Report exposure time, changes and actions taken.

ito-guide--first-aid-infection.mu.content:
>Spotting a worsening wound
Check wounds again during a prolonged wait for care.
1. Write down the injury time and what contaminated it, such as soil, floodwater or a bite. At dressing changes check for increasing warmth, swelling, redness, pain, discharge or fever.
2. Seek prompt medical advice for suspected infection, especially if changes are spreading or the person feels generally unwell. Keep the wound clean and covered. Do not squeeze, cut or try to drain it.
3. Confusion, difficult breathing or a rapid decline is an emergency. Report the wound plus the change in the person's condition.
4. Keep a record of temperature if available, dressing changes and symptoms. Do not rely on colour alone or wait for every sign to appear.

ito-guide--first-aid-monitor.mu.content:
>Monitoring someone awaiting care
Record changes and restart the emergency assessment whenever the person deteriorates.
1. Note the time, injury or illness, response to voice, whether breathing is normal, major bleeding and treatment already given. Ask about relevant health conditions and medicines if the person can answer.
2. Stay with them and recheck regularly, particularly after moving or changing a dressing. Compare findings with the last check rather than relying on memory.
3. Act on a worsening response, abnormal breathing or renewed severe bleeding. Restart assessment, call or update emergency services, and treat immediate threats.
4. Give rescuers the timeline, changes and first aid already performed. Avoid giving food or drink when swallowing is impaired or shock is suspected.

ito-guide--first-aid-shock.mu.content:
>Recognising circulatory shock
Treat shock as life-threatening, especially after serious bleeding or injury.
1. Look for pale or clammy skin, fast breathing, weakness, dizziness or declining response. Call for emergency help early. Control severe bleeding immediately.
2. Help the person lie down if tolerated and safe. If breathing or injury makes that difficult, keep them still in the position that best supports breathing. Keep them warm with a dry covering.
3. Do not give food or drink. Continue to check response and breathing, and note changes with times. Look again for bleeding if the condition worsens.
4. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Report the cause if known and the trend in breathing and responsiveness.

ito-guide--first-aid-supplies.mu.content:
>First aid supplies
Keep a first aid kit accessible, dry and easy to take with you.

Include disposable gloves, sterile dressings, assorted plasters, bandages, medical tape, a thermometer, antiseptic, sterile eyewash and tweezers. Keep a written list and emergency phone numbers with it.
Plan for prescribed medicines and equipment your household depends on, such as diabetes supplies. Store medicines safely away from children and follow their storage instructions. Check supplies and expiry dates at least every six months; replace used or damaged sterile items.
A practical first aid course helps you use the kit and respond while emergency help is on its way.

ito-guide--first-aid-wounds.mu.content:
>Cleaning and dressing a minor wound
Only clean a minor wound after bleeding is controlled.
1. Wash your hands and use gloves if available. Stop bleeding with pressure. A deep wound, severe bleeding or embedded object needs medical care rather than field cleaning.
2. Rinse with clean tap water, bottled water or sterile saline. Clean the surrounding skin with soap and water, keeping soap and harsh disinfectant out of the wound. Do not dig out debris.
3. Pat the surrounding skin dry, cover with a sterile dressing or plaster, and replace it if wet or dirty. Keep the dressing clean and check the site when changing it.
4. Seek advice for bites, deep or persistently dirty wounds, or an uncertain tetanus vaccination history. Watch for increasing pain, redness, warmth, swelling or pus.

ito-guide--food-cooking.mu.content:
>Cooking without mains power
Choose a cooking method based on available safe water, fuel and ventilation.
1. Start with ready-to-eat food if there is no suitable outdoor cooking site. Check labels and portion it with clean utensils. Never move a barbecue or camping stove indoors for heat or light.
2. If using an outdoor stove, assemble and test it cold as instructed. Put it on stable level ground away from tents and combustibles. Keep water and food utensils separate from fuel handling.
3. Make a simple one-pot meal with verified safe water and ingredients whose full cooking time fits the fuel available. Use the packet directions and a food probe for foods that need thorough cooking.
4. Turn off the heat and serve promptly. Put equipment away only when cool. If the flame fails, shut off the fuel and follow the appliance instructions before relighting.

ito-guide--food-foraging.mu.content:
>Avoiding poisoning when foraging
Use known safe food when identification, permission or site history is uncertain.
1. Before foraging, verify access and collection rules. Avoid contaminated ground, sprayed verges, protected species and sites where collection is prohibited.
2. Learn with a qualified local expert. Identify the whole individual specimen at its current growth stage and check dangerous lookalikes using reliable local references. A photo app, single feature, smell, animal feeding or folk test cannot establish edibility.
3. If any doubt remains, leave it. Do not taste unidentified plants or fungi. Cooking or drying does not reliably remove poisons.
4. If someone eats a suspect specimen, seek urgent poison advice or emergency care. Save a photo or leftover specimen if safe. Do not make them vomit.

ito-guide--food-fuel-save.mu.content:
>Cooking with limited fuel
Choose meals that stay safe if the fuel supply runs out.
1. List fuel and ready-to-eat food. Prefer meals with small liquid volumes and short cook times. Keep a cold option for when weather, stove condition or fuel rules out cooking.
2. Measure safe water before heating. Use a close-fitting lid and match pan size to the burner. Once boiling, turn down to the heat needed for the recipe. Avoid adding a windscreen around a gas canister unless the manufacturer permits it.
3. Cook only the portion needed. Choose small even pieces for even heating. Check required time or temperature rather than ending cooking early to save fuel.
4. Never leave food undercooked to finish later or use warm insulated storage in place of cooking. If fuel stops before a safe cook is complete, switch to the cold option.

ito-guide--food-hygiene.mu.content:
>Keeping food preparation clean
Set up separate dirty and clean areas before opening food.
1. Wash hands with soap and safe water. Clean the work surface and set one board or tray aside for ready-to-eat food. Keep raw meat and its packaging on a separate tray.
2. Handle clean ingredients first. After touching raw food, wash hands and wash utensils before they touch anything cooked. Do not rinse raw poultry, which can spread contaminated droplets.
3. Cook with verified safe water and use a clean probe if needed. Serve onto a clean plate rather than the one that held raw ingredients.
4. Remove food waste, clean utensils and dry them safely. If the site cannot support safe water and separation, choose a meal requiring less handling.

ito-guide--food-outdoor.mu.content:
>Preparing a meal outdoors
Use a stable setup and choose a meal you can cook and serve in one session.
1. Arrange safe water, soap, clean utensils, probe and waste bag before lighting. Set clean gear on an elevated surface away from raw food and grit.
2. Put the stove outdoors on level ground. Measure the water and prepare a small batch. Use a clean probe in the thickest or coldest part if measuring. UK FSA standard advice is a core temperature of 70°C for two minutes or an equivalent validated combination.
3. Serve immediately with clean utensils. If leftovers cannot be safely chilled, do not keep them for later.
4. When equipment cools, clean with safe water and pack the waste out. Never wash greasy equipment or throw scraps into a water source.

ito-guide--food-planning.mu.content:
>Planning meals from a limited reserve
Build a use order from what is safe, what needs fuel and who needs it.
1. Write down servings and labelled storage needs. Separate safe perishables from ambient food. Record allergies, infant needs and foods people can actually use.
2. Use safely held perishables first. Mark meals needing little water and fuel, and keep some ready-to-eat options for bad weather or equipment failure.
3. For each day, count meals, safe water for cooking, and fuel before opening multiple packs. Adjust portions to avoid leftovers where you cannot refrigerate.
4. Recount after each day or resupply. If cold-chain history is uncertain, do not allocate suspect food. Prioritise a reliable resupply before the shelf-stable buffer is gone.

ito-guide--food-power-cut.mu.content:
>Food safety during a power cut
Keep the doors shut and note when the power went off.

1. Leave the fridge and freezer closed where possible. In UK guidance, a closed fridge may keep food cold for about four hours. A full freezer may stay frozen for up to 48 hours, or 24 hours if half full. These are estimates. Room temperature and repeated opening reduce the time.
2. Use a thermometer. A fridge normally runs at 5°C or below. Under UK outage guidance, once chilled food reaches 8°C, use it within four hours or discard it. If you cannot tell how long it has been too warm and it may have been four hours, discard high-risk foods such as meat, fish, ready meals and leftovers. Restored power does not reverse unsafe storage.
3. Use safely chilled perishables first, then food that can be eaten safely without cooking, then shelf-stable supplies. Keep raw and ready-to-eat food separate. Follow local food safety guidance for thawed food.
4. Never taste food to check its safety. Discard food touched by floodwater. Use camping stoves and barbecues only outdoors.

ito-guide--food-preservation.mu.content:
>Choosing a safe preservation method
Pick a tested method you can complete with the equipment and controls you have.
1. For short interruptions, prefer bought shelf-stable items. Refrigeration and freezing depend on continuously verified cold temperatures.
2. Use tested crop-specific recipes for drying, pickling or canning. Read the equipment, acidity, processing and storage requirements before starting. A substitute ingredient or container size can change safety.
3. Low-acid foods require tested pressure-canning procedures and equipment. A water bath, ordinary pressure cooker or a good-looking seal is not evidence that low-acid food is safe. Avoid makeshift garlic or herb oil preservation.
4. Label batches with process and date. If a seal fails, the method was uncertain or the jar leaks or bulges, do not open it to taste or sniff. Follow disposal guidance.

ito-guide--food-spoilage.mu.content:
>Deciding when food must be discarded
Use storage history and packaging condition to decide what to keep.
1. Check label, use-by date, exposure and temperature history. If a chilled item spent too long warm or could have, discard it. Smell cannot identify all dangerous contamination.
2. Discard leaking, swollen or badly damaged cans and jars, or jars that spurt on opening. Do not taste suspect food or try to rescue it by cooking.
3. Separate flood-exposed or waste-contaminated food and packaging from clean stores. Follow local disposal instructions and wash your hands after handling.
4. Replace stock using a record of what was lost. Keep a thermometer, record the start of outages and inspect packaging at receipt so the next decision depends less on guesswork.

ito-guide--food-storage.mu.content:
>Storing food without refrigeration
Make the main reserve out of foods labelled for ambient storage.
1. Sort unopened shelf-stable foods from products that say to refrigerate. Dry grains, canned foods and shelf-stable meals belong in a cool dry cupboard, away from fuel, floodwater and pests.
2. Group items by type and put those expiring first at the front. Keep packaging directions and allergen information. After opening, follow the label on storage and time limits.
3. If you cannot chill leftovers safely, open or cook only what can be eaten promptly. A cool room, cellar or shaded box is no guarantee of a safe fridge temperature.
4. Seal dry foods against moisture and pests. Check the shelf periodically for insects, leaks and damage. Discard compromised stock without tasting it.

ito-guide--food-stoves.mu.content:
>Using a camping stove safely
Check the fuel connection and outdoor site before lighting.
1. Use the stove and fuel listed by the manufacturer. Inspect seals and fittings for damage. Connect or replace fuel outdoors away from flame with the stove off and cool.
2. Put the stove on a stable non-combustible surface in open air. Keep it away from tents, doors, dry vegetation and people passing. Keep all combustion equipment out of tents, vehicles and enclosed shelters.
3. Stop before lighting if you smell fuel, hear a leak or see a damaged connection. Follow the instructions, and keep ignition sources away. Never test a leak with a flame.
4. Use a pot within the stated size limit and stay with it. Shut fuel off on completion and allow the stove to cool before packing it. Do not improvise around damaged parts.

ito-guide--navigation-bearing.mu.content:
>Following a bearing on foot
Break a bearing into short safe legs between identifiable points.
1. Set the corrected magnetic bearing. Turn until the needle and orienting arrow line up. Pick a visible target straight ahead along the travel arrow, such as a distinctive boulder.
2. Walk to it by safe ground, then stop and repeat. Confirm expected features and distance. In poor visibility choose much shorter legs and use a calibrated pace count only as an estimate.
3. When a hazard crosses the line, stop and choose a known safe alternative or turn back. A precise bearing does not make a steep slope, river or bog passable.
4. Mark a catching feature beyond the target before starting. If you reach it early or never encounter the expected feature, stop and reassess from a known point rather than correcting by guesswork.

ito-guide--navigation-cold-water.mu.content:
>Falling into cold water
Float first and let your breathing settle before trying to swim.

If you fall in, try to resist the urge to thrash or swim straight away. Tilt your head back with your ears in the water and breathe normally. Spread your arms and legs and move your hands gently if needed to stay afloat. Your legs may sink while your mouth stays above water.

Once breathing settles, call for help. Swim towards safety only if you are able and can reach it safely.

If you see someone in trouble, call local emergency services. In the UK call 999 or 112. At the coast ask for Coastguard. Inland, tell the operator it is a water rescue and where it is. In Scotland, ask for Police Scotland. Keep sight of the person, stay on land and follow the dispatcher.

ito-guide--navigation-compass.mu.content:
>Taking a compass bearing
Use a baseplate compass to transfer a direction from a map.
1. Confirm start and target. Put the edge along their connecting line, with the travel arrow pointing from start to target. Leave the compass flat.
2. Turn the dial until the internal north lines run parallel to the map's north-south grid lines and the north mark points north. Read the index at the travel arrow. This is a grid bearing.
3. Use the current local grid-to-magnetic conversion and the sign shown on the map or reliable offline reference. If magnetic north is 2 degrees east of grid north, for example, subtract 2 from the grid bearing to set a magnetic bearing.
4. Away from metal and electronics, rotate your body until the north needle sits in the orienting arrow. Check the route is safe before following the travel arrow. A result near 180 degrees off usually means the compass was reversed.

ito-guide--navigation-grid.mu.content:
>Reading a UK grid reference
Use the British National Grid letters plus eastings then northings.
1. Locate the labelled 100 km square letters on the relevant map and choose the 1 km grid square containing your position.
2. Read the two figures of the vertical grid line on the left, then the two figures of the horizontal line below. In a hypothetical square marked 23 and 45, with letters SK, this gives SK 2345.
3. Estimate tenths of the square rightwards and then upwards. Three tenths east and six tenths north gives SK 233 456. A six-figure grid reference describes a 100 m square.
4. Send the letters, digits and format. Add a nearby feature and how certain you are. If the position comes from a phone confirm it is set to British National Grid. Latitude and longitude are a separate format.

ito-guide--navigation-lost.mu.content:
>What to do when lost
Stop somewhere safe and keep the group together.

1. Mark the last location you can confidently identify and how long ago you passed it. Check the map and compass against landmarks you can see now. If your phone gives a position, record the grid reference or coordinates and check that they match the terrain.
2. Only retrace your route if you recognise it and can safely travel it. Do not descend into unknown steep ground or cross water to take a shortcut. If visibility or weather worsens, shelter where safe and add dry layers.
3. If you are injured or cannot safely get out, contact local rescue early. In the UK call 999 or 112. In the hills ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue. At the coast ask for Coastguard.
4. Give your best position, last known point, nearby landmarks, group size, injuries and a callback number. Save phone power and stay contactable. Stay where the rescue team expects you unless you must move away from danger. Tell rescuers if you move.

ito-guide--navigation-maps.mu.content:
>Reading a map
Identify scale, north and recognisable features before moving.
1. Read the legend and contour interval. At 1:25,000, one centimetre on paper is 250 metres on the ground. Measure a winding route in short segments rather than straight between endpoints.
2. Orient the sheet to terrain or a compass. Find a reliable starting feature such as a junction, bridge or distinct ridge. Confirm it with another feature, including its direction or height.
3. Trace the route and mark decision points, escape routes, steep slopes and obstacles. Look for the next expected feature before you leave the current one.
4. If the map and landscape disagree, stop. Recheck scale, alignment and your last known point. Maps may omit fences, flood damage or recent path changes. Never assume a mapped path is currently passable.

ito-guide--navigation-route.mu.content:
>Planning a safe walking route
Write an offline route card before committing to exposed terrain.
1. Mark start, destination, distinct checkpoints, turning points and safer alternatives on a paper map. For each leg note distance, ascent, terrain, likely time and the feature that marks the end.
2. Check weather, tide if relevant, daylight and group capacity. Choose a conservative turnaround time that leaves time to return safely. Add margins for poor footing and navigation stops.
3. Share the route, change options and overdue action with someone who can raise help. Carry a copy accessible in rain.
4. At each checkpoint compare actual time, weather and the slowest person's condition with the plan. Turn back or use the escape option before reaching a hazard. Update the contact if the route changes and a connection is available.

ito-guide--navigation-signal.mu.content:
>Signalling for help outdoors
Choose a signal rescuers can detect from your safe position.
1. Where voice carries poorly, use a whistle. At night use a torch with a spare battery. In the UK hills, use six blasts or flashes, wait one minute, and repeat. Other regions may use different patterns.
2. Leave gaps to listen and look for replies. Continue signalling after a reply if it is safe, so a team can find the source. Do not follow an answering sound towards a hazardous slope or river.
3. During daylight, place a bright item against contrasting ground near your position. Keep it secured against wind.
4. If there are several people, assign someone to signal while others care for the casualty and preserve a charged phone or radio for contact. Avoid smoke signals where fire could spread.

ito-guide--navigation-terrain.mu.content:
>Reading terrain from contours
Read the pattern of contours, then verify it on the ground.
1. Find the contour interval and labelled heights. Close lines indicate steeper slopes; more widely spaced lines indicate gentler ground. Closed contours with increasing heights inward usually show a hill.
2. Look for high ridges between valleys and lower saddles between tops. In a stream valley contours often bend uphill. Check heights and water symbols before assuming every bend is a valley.
3. Predict what each leg should look like: uphill or downhill, slope on one side, and a recognisable end point. Compare more than one feature to guard against matching the wrong valley.
4. Avoid relying on contour spacing alone near cliffs, scree and peat. Small hazardous features can be below the map's resolution. If sight and mapping disagree, stop and take a safer route.

ito-guide--navigation-without-gps.mu.content:
>Navigating without GPS
Use a paper map, compass and frequent position checks.
1. Start at a confirmed point and orient the map. Choose a route with features easy to identify in the expected visibility. Use a track or wall as a handrail when it leads safely towards the target.
2. Write the bearing and expected distance for each leg. Know which obvious feature will tell you that you have gone too far. Confirm at every junction rather than waiting until you are lost.
3. Calibrate how many double steps you take over a known distance on safe ground. Use this only for rough range in poor visibility; slopes and rough surfaces change stride.
4. If no two features fit your estimate, stop. Return to the last known point only by a recognised safe route or shelter and signal for help. Avoid relying on moss, guessed sun direction or the slope of a stream to fix position.

ito-guide--power-battery-safety.mu.content:
>Charging and storing batteries
Use the manufacturer’s charger or an approved compatible replacement.

Keep batteries and chargers dry, uncovered and away from bedding, heat, combustible materials and escape routes. Follow the manufacturer’s temperature and storage instructions. Do not charge while asleep or away from home. Protect batteries from crushing, puncture or immersion.
If a battery swells, becomes unusually hot, leaks or smells unusual, stop use and disconnect charging if safe. Do not open or repair the pack; contact the manufacturer or a qualified technician. If it starts smoking or catches fire, get out, stay out and call 999. Do not breathe the fumes or attempt to carry a burning battery outside.
Do not put batteries in household rubbish: use an appropriate battery recycling collection.

ito-guide--power-capacity.mu.content:
>Battery capacity and power
Watt-hours describe stored energy; watts describe the rate at which a device uses it.

A battery rated 500 Wh stores up to about 500 watt-hours when full. A 10 W load running for 10 hours uses about 100 Wh. Estimate energy by multiplying watts by hours, and add the needs of all devices. Manufacturers’ capacity is not all available at the socket: conversion losses, the battery condition and cut-off limits reduce usable energy.
Watts also matter: a unit may have enough stored energy but be unable to supply a high-power appliance. Motors can need a higher starting surge. Check continuous output, starting limits and compatibility; never assume a pump will start from its running watts alone.
Milliamp-hours alone are not comparable across different voltages: Wh = mAh × volts ÷ 1,000.

ito-guide--power-electrical.mu.content:
>Electrical danger during an outage
Keep clear of fallen power lines: assume they are live.

Do not touch a cable or anything in contact with it. Keep others away and report it to the electricity network operator on 105 in Great Britain. Call 999 for immediate danger or if a road or path is blocked.
Never touch electrical equipment with wet hands or while standing in water. Do not use damaged cables, overloaded sockets or improvised adapters. Keep power stations and electrical connections dry. If someone receives an electric shock, do not touch them until the power is safely isolated; call 999.
Never backfeed household wiring from a generator, battery or vehicle through a socket. Have a qualified electrician design and install any household backup connection and protective isolation.

ito-guide--power-generator.mu.content:
>Using a fuel generator safely
Operate outdoors in open air. Carbon monoxide can kill without warning.

1. Choose a dry outdoor site at least 6.1 metres (20 feet) from doors, windows and air vents. Point the exhaust away from buildings. Check where fumes could travel, including towards neighbours. Never run it in a garage, shed, carport or other enclosed or partly enclosed space.
2. Keep working carbon monoxide alarms in the home. If poisoning is suspected, get everyone into fresh air and seek urgent medical help. Stay outside until advised it is safe to return.
3. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for weather protection, loads and suitable leads. Stop the generator and let it cool before refuelling.
4. Never plug the generator into a wall socket to power the house. A qualified electrician must design and install any connection to fixed wiring with the correct changeover and isolation.

ito-guide--power-loads.mu.content:
>Prioritising electrical loads
List essential loads and estimate both their energy use and peak power.

Start with medically necessary equipment and its agreed backup plan, then communication, lighting, essential water and food storage. Record each device’s watts, hours per day, connector and any starting surge. Add watts for things running together and watt-hours over the period they are needed.
Switch off non-essential loads and use a torch instead of lighting whole rooms. A heater, kettle or cooker can use a large amount of energy quickly. Fridges and pumps may cycle automatically and draw a high starting surge: test compatibility, not just the stated running wattage.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed and follow food safety guidance. Reserve enough power for urgent communication.

ito-guide--power-medical.mu.content:
>Power for medical equipment
If loss of power puts someone in immediate danger, call 999.

Before an outage, discuss a written backup and escalation plan with the person’s clinical team and equipment provider. Identify the correct backup supply, how long it lasts, any alarms or switching delay, safe storage of medicines and when to seek help. Test only as directed by the provider.
Ask the electricity supplier and network operator about the Priority Services Register and tell them about electricity-dependent equipment. Registration provides extra support but does not guarantee uninterrupted electricity or immediate restoration.
Keep the provider’s emergency number, contacts and plan on paper. Battery or power-station output compatibility, capacity and changeover must be confirmed for the specific equipment; do not assume a generic unit is suitable.

ito-guide--power-runtime.mu.content:
>Estimating battery runtime
Estimate runtime using usable watt-hours divided by the device’s average watts.

Example: if a battery can deliver 400 Wh at its output and a device averages 20 W, the ideal estimate is 400 ÷ 20 = 20 hours. Actual runtime can be shorter because of inverter overhead, changing loads, cold, battery age or automatic shutdown. The usable figure may be much lower than the advertised battery capacity; measure it with the real setup.
Include all loads, such as the router, radio and host computer. A fridge or pump cycles and may need a large starting surge; its label alone does not establish average consumption or successful start-up.
Leave a reserve and test safely before an outage. Do not rely on estimates for life-support equipment.

ito-guide--power-solar-home.mu.content:
>Home solar during a power cut
Do not assume rooftop solar will power your home when the grid fails.

Many grid-connected solar systems shut down during a power cut for safety. A suitable inverter and properly configured backup or island-mode installation are needed for the circuits intended to operate independently. A battery alone does not guarantee backup capability or an uninterrupted changeover.
Check your own system’s documentation and ask its installer which sockets or circuits remain powered, how switching works, what it can start and whether solar can recharge the battery during an outage. Test in advance with qualified guidance.
Never alter wiring, bypass protective equipment or feed a generator or power station into a wall socket. Household backup and grid isolation require a qualified electrician.

ito-guide--power-solar-portable.mu.content:
>Charging from portable solar
Match the array and cable to the station's labelled input limits.
1. Read the station's solar voltage, current, permitted wattage, polarity and connector requirements. Use approved equipment. The array's cold-weather open-circuit voltage must stay within the input limit. Ask the manufacturer if any figure is uncertain.
2. Set the panel on firm ground with a clear view of the sun. Secure it from wind and protect the station from rain. Follow the required connection and disconnection order.
3. Read actual input watts after connection. If low, check shade, angle and connectors. Estimate energy from measured power and expected generating hours, allowing for clouds and losses.
4. Disconnect using the instructions if leads are damaged or conditions are unsafe. Never improvise a mains connection or depend on nameplate solar output alone.

ito-guide--power-station.mu.content:
>Using a portable power station
Test a portable station with its intended loads before depending on it.
1. Record energy capacity in watt-hours and maximum continuous and surge outputs. Compare the load and its starting surge with those limits. Use the correct port and cable.
2. Connect essential loads one at a time. Read measured wattage after startup. Estimate duration from usable watt-hours divided by running watts, allowing for losses and the station's own draw.
3. Stop if a plug is loose, the station shows a fault or it becomes unexpectedly hot. Keep it dry, ventilated, away from exits and within the manufacturer's temperature limits.
4. Never connect its output to fixed wiring or a wall socket. Arrange specialist backup for medical loads. Keep an independent reserve for the most important task.

>Emergency evacuation
Leave promptly when instructed or when staying places you in immediate danger.

Take medicines, essential medical equipment, phone, charger, keys, identification, warm clothing, drinking water and supplies for children and pets if time allows. Tell someone where you are going. Follow the emergency services’ route and instructions.
If leaving due to flooding, turn off gas, electricity and water only if safe and instructed. Never walk or drive through floodwater. Do not touch electrical equipment while standing in water.
Keep a grab bag and a written list of essential contacts. Do not return until authorities say it is safe.

ito-guide--preparedness-flood.mu.content:
>Preparing for flooding
Move people to safety early and keep your route clear of floodwater.

Before the water rises, identify a safe route to higher ground and where you can stay. Keep medicines, phone, power bank, torch and essentials together. Move pets and key belongings upstairs if safe. In England, arrange to receive Environment Agency flood warnings where available. Use the relevant local warning service elsewhere.

During flooding, follow evacuation instructions and leave early if your route is safe. Never walk, cycle or drive through floodwater. If trapped, move upstairs or to another higher safe place and call emergency services. In the UK call 999. Give the address, where you are in the building and who needs help. Avoid going into an attic without an escape route. Only isolate utilities if you can safely reach dry controls. Do not touch electrical switches while standing in water.

After flooding, follow official instructions about returning. Leave affected gas and electrical systems off until checked by qualified professionals. Use a confirmed safe water supply if your usual supply might be contaminated.

Keep essential supplies together where everyone can find them.

Include safe drinking water, ready-to-eat food and a manual tin opener, torch, spare batteries, battery or wind-up radio, power bank, first aid supplies, hygiene items and essential medicines.
Plan at least 3 litres of drinking water per person per day; allow more for cooking, hygiene and individual needs. Include baby supplies, mobility or medical equipment, pet food, warm clothing and copies of important numbers.

ito-guide--preparedness-priorities.mu.content:
>Making decisions when stranded
Pause, get everyone safe, and choose the next action from what you can verify.
1. Stop at a safe position. Check injuries, exposure, daylight, the last reliable location and who knows your route. Have someone write down what you know and what you are guessing.
2. Divide jobs: first aid, shelter, communication and maintaining a record. Put the next check-in and turnaround time in writing. Give a cold or frightened person a small feasible task if they are able.
3. Compare staying with moving. If the route out is uncertain or would expose people to worse hazards, shelter and signal. If the current site is dangerous, move the shortest safe distance away and record the new position.
4. Recheck when weather changes, a task stalls or someone deteriorates. Replace a failed plan early rather than using dwindling daylight, power or energy to pursue it.

If water or sewage services fail, follow the water company and local authority instructions.

Keep drinking water separate from water used for flushing. If the sewer system is working and local advice permits, non-drinking water can be used for flushing. If told not to flush because sewage services have failed, do not flush.
For a national outage, UK public health guidance advises collecting faeces in plastic bags, sealing them and placing them in an outside household waste bin; follow any different local disposal instructions. Keep waste away from food, children, animals and water sources.
Wash hands with soap and safe water after using the toilet and before food preparation. Use sanitiser if handwashing is unavailable. Avoid contact with sewage and floodwater.

Keep away from fallen power lines and anything touching them; assume they are live. Report a power cut or dangerous electricity equipment on 105 in Great Britain, and call 999 for immediate danger. Never use generators or camping stoves indoors.

ito-guide--sanitation-bathing.mu.content:
>Personal hygiene without running water
Use small batches of safe water and keep used water out of the clean container.
1. Pour enough safe water into a personal wash basin. Keep a separate clean supply for teeth, wound care and any care requiring clean water.
2. Wash less soiled skin first and more soiled areas last, with soap and a personal cloth. Dry skin folds and feet well. Do not share towels, cloths or toothbrushes.
3. Use clean hands and a clean surface when changing dressings or menstrual products. Bag waste according to the local arrangement and wash hands afterwards.
4. Empty used water where local rules permit, away from the drinking supply. Clean and dry the basin. Do not use water suspected of sewage or chemical contamination.

ito-guide--sanitation-camp.mu.content:
>Keeping a temporary camp sanitary
Separate the clean water and cooking area from toilets, waste and laundry.
1. Walk the site and check where runoff goes before placing facilities. Keep toilets and waste away from water sources and flood paths. Use designated facilities where available.
2. Place a handwash station at the toilet and make safe water and soap available at the kitchen. Mark clean water clearly. Keep dirty tools and water containers in their own area.
3. Assign someone to check bag capacity, water, soap and waste storage daily. Keep bins closed and remove sealed waste on the agreed route.
4. If someone has diarrhoea or vomiting, keep them away from food preparation, use separate personal items where possible, and clean soiled surfaces. Review water and food handling immediately.

ito-guide--sanitation-disposal.mu.content:
>Containing and disposing of human waste
Set up a route for waste before relying on a temporary toilet.
1. Use functioning toilets or designated collections first. In the field, carry an approved human-waste pack-out kit where no facility is available. Follow its sealing and disposal instructions.
2. At home, place sealed bags in a covered leak-resistant container, away from food, children, animals and floodwater. Mark it clearly. Confirm how the local authority wants it collected.
3. Never dump waste into streams, drains, pits near water or ordinary recycling. Local rules may require pack-out and can prohibit burial.
4. If a bag leaks, keep people away, use gloves to enclose it in a new bag and clean the affected surface according to local public health guidance. Wash hands with safe water immediately afterwards.

ito-guide--sanitation-hands.mu.content:
>Handwashing with a small water supply
Provide flowing safe water from a tap container or a helper pouring a jug.
1. Place soap and a drying option next to the water. Catch used water in a separate basin where runoff would reach the camp or source. Keep the clean-water tap away from dirty hands where possible.
2. Wet hands, turn off flow and lather. Rub palms, backs, thumbs, between fingers and under nails for at least 20 seconds. Rinse with flowing safe water and dry.
3. Wash after using the toilet, changing nappies or handling waste, and before preparing food or caring for a wound.
4. Alcohol hand sanitiser of at least 60 percent is a fallback when soap and safe water are unavailable. It does not work well on visibly dirty hands or against every germ. Wash as soon as practical.

ito-guide--sanitation-laundry.mu.content:
>Handling contaminated clothing and equipment
Separate soiled items at the point of use and handle them as little as possible.
1. Wear suitable gloves. Put wet or visibly soiled equipment in a marked leak-resistant bag. Keep it away from bedding, food and clean water. Avoid shaking clothing.
2. Follow local flood or health advice for sewage contamination. Launder washable items with detergent as their labels permit and dry fully. Keep raw laundry off food surfaces and do not reuse its water.
3. Clean hard equipment first, then disinfect if indicated using a compatible product at its labelled dilution and contact time. Never mix cleaning chemicals.
4. Discard items that cannot be cleaned safely. Wash hands after removing gloves. For fuel or unknown chemicals, isolate the item and obtain qualified advice instead of laundering it at home.

ito-guide--sanitation-toilet.mu.content:
>Setting up an emergency toilet
Switch to containment if the sewer or septic system cannot safely take flushes.
Equipment: stable lidded bucket or dry toilet bowl, strong bags, absorbent and a handwashing station.
1. Use a working toilet elsewhere if available. If local advice says do not flush, mark the household toilet to stop accidental use. Set the temporary toilet on a level private surface.
2. Line the bucket with two bags and secure their rims. Add a small amount of suitable absorbent. Fit a stable seat if available and keep the lid shut between uses.
3. Before the inner bag becomes heavy, close it without squeezing and seal in the outer bag. Put it in a separate covered, pest-resistant container. Follow local collection and disposal directions.
4. Wash hands after every use and clean the seat and bucket when soiled. Keep this setup away from food and drinking water.

ito-guide--sanitation-waste.mu.content:
>Managing solid waste and wash water
Plan how to remove waste before it attracts animals or reaches water.
1. Separate food scraps, ordinary packaging, sanitary waste and sharp or hazardous items. Keep each in a suitable labelled container. Keep batteries and chemicals out of wet refuse and follow local disposal rules.
2. Scrape food into a closed food-waste container before washing utensils. Strain out scraps if washing outside. Pack them out with the rest of the rubbish.
3. Dispose of wash water only where allowed and away from water bodies, sources and drains that lead to streams. Use designated sinks or collection at established sites.
4. Inspect storage for leaks, pests and rainwater entry. Never burn plastic, batteries or sanitary waste. Leave the site with every bag and loose item accounted for.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-growing.mu.content:
>Starting a small reliable food garden
Start at a scale you can water and maintain.
1. Choose a sunny accessible spot with safe soil or containers and clean compost. Check drainage and shelter before buying plants. Avoid growing edible crops directly in soil with suspected contamination.
2. Pick a few crops suited to the season and space, using packet spacing and depth. Sow small staggered batches for a more continuous harvest.
3. Water the root zone and check containers often in dry weather. Mulch where appropriate. Change the watering schedule based on soil moisture rather than the calendar alone.
4. Record sowing, germination and harvest. If a crop fails, check moisture, temperature, spacing and pest damage before resowing. Keep a food reserve while crops establish.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-maintenance..content:
>Maintaining essential equipment
Test the equipment in the state it will be used, including spares.
1. Make a list of essential gear and the task each item supports. Check handles, hinges, seals and connectors under good light. Tag faults before equipment goes back into storage.
2. Clean soil and moisture from hand tools, dry them and follow the maker's guidance on lubricating or protecting metal. Replace split handles, cracked blades and unsafe parts.
3. Test torches and radios with the intended batteries and cables. Keep instructions where you store the device. Check expiry and packaging on sterile supplies.
4. Quarantine faults you cannot verify. Do not repair mains wiring, gas equipment or damaged battery packs yourself. Record what is out of service and its backup.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-outage.mu.content:
>Managing a prolonged infrastructure outage
Reassess people, shelter, safe water and communications before each new work period.
1. Write a short status board with usable supplies, expected resupply, people needing extra help and outstanding hazards. Assign each task and when it needs checking again.
2. Decide when staying becomes unsafe, such as loss of essential medical power, safe water or warmth. Identify a safe destination and route before reaching that point. Keep options available for people who cannot travel easily.
3. Pair up for risky trips. Leave the route and latest return time with someone who will act if you are overdue. Rotate tiring work and use a written handover.
4. At each check, compare actual resources with the thresholds. Change the plan when assumptions fail rather than spending time or power on a procedure you cannot finish safely.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-rain-system..content:
>Setting up a non-potable rainwater store
Use a covered water butt for suitable non-drinking jobs.
1. Put a suitable tank on a level base rated for the filled weight. Keep it stable and away from places where an overflow would flood the building or undermine the base.
2. Fit a covered inlet with a removable screen and route overflow to a suitable place. Secure the lid against children, animals and insects. Label outlet and stored water as non-potable.
3. Keep the system physically separate from drinking-water plumbing. Check after rain for leaks, blocked screens and unsafe overflow. Follow the tank's cold-weather instructions.
4. Use the water only for suitable tasks. A screen or first flush cannot remove all contaminants. Keep untreated roof water away from drinking, food preparation and wound care.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-repairs.mu.content:
>Temporary repairs to fabric and gear
Repair low-consequence damage first, such as a torn bag or tarp.
1. Take the item out of load and dry it. Trim loose dirt and keep the fabric flat. Align a small tear edge to edge without pulling it larger.
2. Apply compatible repair tape to clean fabric, rounding its corners and extending it beyond the tear. Press from the centre out. Follow the material's instructions before applying tension or wetting.
3. Test gently in a sheltered place. Reduce load or move tension to a sound attachment point if the repair lifts. Keep a backup cover available.
4. Treat temporary repairs as temporary. Replace failed structural points. Do not patch climbing equipment, safety harnesses, gas lines or electrical insulation for continued use.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-seeds.mu.content:
>Saving seed for the next growing season
Start with a healthy familiar crop and a variety likely to breed true.
1. Choose open-pollinated stock where a similar next generation matters. Hybrids can vary and cross-pollinating crops may need isolation. Mark healthy plants before harvest.
2. Let suitable dry seed heads mature on the plant. Collect when dry, before they shed. Separate loose debris and finish drying indoors out of direct heat. Wet-seeded crops need their own method.
3. Label species, variety and year. Store thoroughly dry seed in labelled envelopes in a cool dry place, protected from pests.
4. Test a small batch before depending on it for a season. Discard mouldy seed and do not eat seed intended for planting.

>Maintaining a working stock of supplies
Record how much you can use before the next safe resupply.
1. List usable servings, litres, essential hygiene items and equipment consumables. Keep food labels and note use-by dates, opening dates and any damaged packaging.
2. Put supplies in rotation. Place earlier safe dates at the front, and use regular meals to turn stock over. Keep one ready-to-use buffer separate from items that need fuel or water.
3. Set a refill point for each essential item from the household's normal use and realistic resupply time. Record what was taken during an interruption.
4. Check after rain, heat, pests or power loss. Separate suspect food or water at once. Recount actual usable stocks before deciding what can be shared or used.

ito-guide--self-sufficiency-water.mu.content:
>Running separate potable and utility supplies
Use two sets of containers and track both reserves.
1. Draw a simple flow diagram from each supply to its uses. Reserve potable water for drinking, food and essential hygiene. Mark non-potable outlets, hoses and buckets so they are hard to confuse.
2. Give each supply a dedicated scoop or tap. Store clean containers capped and off contaminated surfaces. Never make a temporary cross-connection with drinking-water plumbing.
3. Measure use for a day and adjust the reserve. Schedule high-volume non-essential jobs around known resupply. Use utility water for permitted tasks only.
4. If a cross-contact occurs, stop using the affected potable reserve until it can be replaced or assessed. Protect the remaining safe supply from the suspect equipment.

ito-guide--shelter-alarms.mu.content:
>Smoke, heat and CO alarms
Working alarms give early warning. Test them regularly and keep exits clear.

Fit smoke alarms in rooms where a fire may start, except the kitchen, where a heat alarm is more suitable. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for location, testing, maintenance and replacement. Never remove batteries to silence an alarm without restoring protection.
Fit an audible carbon monoxide alarm in each room containing an appliance burning gas, oil, coal or wood. A carbon monoxide alarm is not a smoke alarm. Maintain appliances, chimneys and ventilation; an alarm does not replace maintenance.
Make and practise an escape plan, including help for anyone who cannot escape unaided. Ask your local fire and rescue service for tailored home safety advice.

ito-guide--shelter-camping.mu.content:
>Tent and camping fire safety
Keep stoves, heaters, barbecues and flames out of tents and enclosed shelters.

Fuel-burning equipment can cause fire and deadly carbon monoxide, even where you cannot smell smoke. A barbecue can remain dangerous after cooking: never bring it inside to cool or warm a shelter. Use a battery torch rather than a candle.
Cook outside, away from tent walls, long grass and other flammable material. Follow appliance and campsite instructions. Store fuel and gas cylinders outside the tent, away from heat, and keep children away.
Know the campsite emergency arrangements and how to escape the tent. If fire spreads, get everyone away and call 999. If clothes catch fire: stop, drop and roll.
