>Carbon monoxide poisoning
If you suspect carbon monoxide, get outside into fresh air immediately.

Stop using the suspected appliance if you can do so safely. Do not go back inside until advised it is safe. Carbon monoxide has no smell or colour. Headache, dizziness, nausea and weakness can be signs; symptoms may improve outside or affect several people.
Call 999 if an exposed person has difficulty breathing, confusion, loss of consciousness, weakness, chest pain or muscle pain. For other suspected symptoms, call NHS 111 promptly. If you suspect a gas appliance is leaking carbon monoxide, call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999.
Never use a barbecue, camping stove or generator indoors, in a tent or garage. Fit an audible carbon monoxide alarm in each room containing a fuel-burning appliance, and maintain appliances and flues.

ito-guide--shelter-debris.mu.content:
>Low shelter with natural insulation
Use dry loose debris as supplementary insulation where collection is allowed.
1. Prefer a tarp, bivvy or carried emergency shelter. Pick a dry safe site. If using an existing low sturdy support, check it will not roll or fall. Avoid placing yourself underneath heavy branches or slabs.
2. Create a low cover with a tarp or light ribs resting against that support. Use only low loads and leave an opening large enough to exit. In a pinch, light dry leaves or grass can be layered over light ribs for wind protection where permitted. Wet material adds load and loses insulation.
3. Put a separate thick dry layer or mat underneath you and keep your face clear. Check for insects, sharp debris and dampness. Keep ventilation and the exit open.
4. Abandon an unstable, leaking or compressing structure. Avoid dismantling living vegetation. Never use flame in or beside dry debris.

ito-guide--shelter-emergency.mu.content:
>Emergency outdoor shelter
Get away from immediate hazards, take shelter and call for help early.

1. Stop where the group can safely gather, out of wind and away from rising streams, steep drops and falling rock. Avoid making a difficult descent or river crossing just to reach a building.
2. Put a mat or spare clothing between people and the ground. Add dry layers, then a windproof outer layer, bivvy bag or group shelter. Get out of the rain before stripping off wet layers. Keep faces clear and never light a stove or flame inside the shelter.
3. Check everyone for confusion, slurred speech or unusual drowsiness. Suspected hypothermia needs emergency help. Keep the group together and monitor anyone who is injured or cold.
4. Give rescuers your last reliable location, a grid reference if possible, nearby features, the number of people and injuries, and a callback number. UK hills: dial 999 or 112, ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue. UK coast: ask for Coastguard. Stay where rescuers expect you unless you must move to safety. Tell them if you move.

ito-guide--shelter-ground.mu.content:
>Insulating yourself from the ground
Build the layer beneath you before adding more blankets above.
1. Start on safe dry ground sheltered from the wind. Remove sharp stones that could puncture a mat. Avoid a depression where rainwater collects.
2. Use an insulated sleeping mat. If there is none, lay spare dry clothing, empty packs or other dry non-sharp materials beneath your trunk and hips. Spread weight and use a dry barrier if the surface is damp.
3. Lie down and check for cold spots and material compressing flat. Add insulation where weight bears on the ground. Keep spare dry clothing available for the person who needs it most.
4. Check anyone who cannot adjust their position or tell you they are cold. A foil sheet helps block wind and wet but supplies little cushioning or insulation on its own.

ito-guide--shelter-heat-prevention.mu.content:
>Staying safe in extreme heat
Move to a cooler place, drink regularly and watch for signs of heat illness.

Close curtains or blinds against direct sun. If it is hotter outside, close windows during the day and ventilate when it is cooler and safe to do so. Wear loose light clothing, rest in the shade and avoid strenuous activity in the hottest part of the day. Never leave children or animals in a parked car.
Check on people at higher risk, including older people, young children and people with long-term illness. Follow individual medical advice about fluid restrictions.
Confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures or breathing difficulty in a hot person needs 999. Start cooling immediately. If the person remains unwell after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids, call 999.

ito-guide--shelter-house-fire.mu.content:
>Fire in your home
Warn others. If you can escape safely, get out, stay out and call 999.

Do not stop for belongings or try to fight the fire. Close doors behind you if possible. Use stairs, not lifts. In smoke, keep low. Before opening a door, check it with the back of your hand; do not open it if warm.
If you cannot escape safely, go to a room as far from fire and smoke as possible, close the door, block gaps with soft material, call 999 and tell the operator where you are. Go to a window if safe and follow their instructions.
For a fire elsewhere in a purpose-built block, follow your building’s evacuation plan and fire service instructions. If fire, smoke or heat affects your flat, leave if safe. Never re-enter a burning building.

ito-guide--shelter-insulation.mu.content:
>Keeping heat in safely
Reduce draughts and use dry layers, while keeping essential ventilation clear.

Close curtains at dusk and internal doors to keep warmth in occupied rooms. Use draught excluders at doors and wear several light layers. Sit on a cushion or folded blanket rather than directly on a cold floor, and use dry bedding.
Do not block fixed air vents, chimneys or flues: fuel-burning appliances need ventilation and can produce carbon monoxide. Keep fabric and bedding away from heaters and open fires. Maintain a clear escape route.
If the house cannot be kept safely warm, seek help and a warmer place. Confusion, drowsiness or slurred speech in a cold person needs urgent action: call 999 for suspected hypothermia.

ito-guide--shelter-lean-to.mu.content:
>Pitching a tarp lean-to
Use a sloping tarp for short-term shelter where wind direction is steady.
1. At a safe site, secure the upper edge at a modest height on two sound supports. Stake the opposite edge low into the wind. Aim the open side away from prevailing rain and gusts, with a clear exit.
2. Tension corners separately so water runs off the low edge. Use reinforced loops rather than puncturing the sheet. Keep the ground mat wholly beneath the cover so it does not catch runoff.
3. Place yourself and dry gear away from the dripping edge. Check air flow, stakes and fabric clearance when lying down.
4. If wind shifts into the opening or drives rain sideways, lower the pitch or change to an A-frame. Do not block the exit or light a fire in or directly in front of the shelter.

ito-guide--shelter-outdoor-fire.mu.content:
>Lighting a fire outdoors
Avoid lighting a fire when there is wildfire risk or local rules prohibit it.

A cold meal and extra layers are safer choices when conditions are dry or windy. Check site rules and local restrictions. Use a fire only where permitted, on a suitable non-flammable surface, well away from tents, buildings, vegetation and other combustible materials.
Keep water or sand nearby and never leave a fire unattended. Do not use petrol or paraffin to light solid fuel. Keep children and pets away. Put the fire completely out and ensure ashes are cold before leaving or disposing of them.
Never take a fire, barbecue or camping stove into a tent or enclosed shelter. If fire spreads, move away and call 999; do not attempt to tackle it.

ito-guide--shelter-prevent-cold.mu.content:
>Preventing hypothermia
Intervene while people can still walk, talk and change clothing normally.
1. Before an exposed stop, add a dry insulating layer and a shell against wind and rain. Use a hat and dry gloves. Avoid sweating into the layers by venting when moving.
2. At a stop, get out of the wind, insulate from the ground and put wet gear somewhere it cannot soak the dry layers. Pack dry reserves separately from the wet kit.
3. Pair people up and check speech, coordination and alertness. Shivering with clumsiness or confusion is a reason to stop travel and reassess. Do not leave a cold person alone.
4. If hypothermia is suspected, handle gently, insulate and seek emergency help as early as you can. Follow the first-aid guide while waiting. Avoid stoves, heaters and flames in enclosed shelter.

ito-guide--shelter-site.mu.content:
>Finding a safe shelter site
Check hazards above, below and uphill before unloading.
1. Look for stable, gently drained ground outside gullies, stream beds, tide reach, flood debris lines and rockfall paths. Avoid steep snow slopes, cliffs and areas where water will run under the shelter.
2. Look up for cracked branches, leaning trees and loose rock. Move away rather than trying to judge whether a damaged branch will hold. Stay clear of lone exposed trees in thunderstorms.
3. Look for a windbreak on safe terrain. Compare conditions on both sides and check whether a wind change would expose the shelter. Stay out of hollows collecting water and avoid exposed ridges.
4. Leave a clear route out, and choose a spot that rescuers can reach or locate. In Britain, use a permitted site when planning a stay. In an emergency, avoid further travel if movement is more dangerous than sheltering.

ito-guide--shelter-tarp.mu.content:
>Pitching an A-frame tarp
Use an A-frame for rain protection when you have secure supports and enough room.
Equipment: tarp with reinforced points, cord, stakes or anchors, and a mat.
1. At a safe site, tension a low ridgeline between two secure supports. Protect tree bark with wide straps if using suitable trees. Keep the line out of paths and do not tension it over a drop.
2. Centre the tarp on the line. Pull the four corners out and down evenly. Keep the windward end low or face it away from the prevailing wind if the terrain allows. Direct drips outside your sleeping area.
3. Lie on your mat to verify clearance from wet fabric. Open an end for ventilation and keep the exit free. Check stakes and pooling again after rain.
4. Lower or dismantle the pitch if supports move or fabric starts tearing. Avoid open flames, stoves and sharp tools under the tarp.

ito-guide--shelter-unsafe-build.mu.content:
>Shelter construction hazards
Reject any build with uncertain structure, ventilation or escape.
1. Test the site first. Avoid unsupported earth cuts, snow banks, unstable dry-stone walls, mines, caves liable to flood, and hollow spaces beneath rock or root plates.
2. Use lightweight cover and known sound supports. Never build a heavy overhead roof out of wet debris, large poles or stone. Avoid using damaged trees and loading branches over people.
3. Keep a visible exit and airflow. Never heat an enclosed shelter with open flames or combustion appliances. Keep cords marked and out of walking routes.
4. Stop if the build needs excavation, tools you cannot use safely, or more time than you have before darkness or bad weather. A group shelter or low tarp on safe ground is usually easier to inspect and abandon.

>Staying warm through a long heating outage
Choose a dry occupied room and reduce avoidable heat loss.
1. Close doors to unused rooms and draw curtains after dark. Keep required vents clear and preserve a safe exit. Use dry clothes, warm bedding and insulation from cold floors.
2. Check on older people, infants and anyone with illness or reduced mobility. If the home cannot stay safely warm, move early to a known heated place while travel is safe.
3. Use electric heating only with suitable equipment, safe sockets and within load limits. Never use a barbecue, camping stove or generator indoors. Keep smoke and CO alarms working.
4. Recheck after dark and before sleeping. Slurred speech, unusual drowsiness or confusion after cold exposure needs urgent assessment, shelter and emergency help.

ito-guide--shelter-weather.mu.content:
>Managing wind and rain in shelter
Recheck the pitch once wind and rain start.
1. Set the shelter low enough to reduce wind loading and check stakes before settling. Make rain run away from your groundsheet. Keep dry gear in a closed bag while moving it under cover.
2. Keep a gap between insulation and wet tarp fabric. Wipe pooling water off from outside if safe, then retension the pitch. Expect some condensation. Open a sheltered end for airflow.
3. Put wet gear in a separate area. Change into dry layers once sheltered and check everyone again after a short interval.
4. If pegs pull, anchor ground softens, a supporting tree moves or water rises, act early. Leave a failing shelter for a verified safer spot rather than trying to hold a loaded line by hand.

If you see an uncontrolled outdoor fire, move away and call 999.

Give the fire service your location and follow its advice. Do not approach the fire, attempt to fight a spreading fire or put yourself in danger to collect belongings. Warn others as you move to safety if you can do so safely.
In dry or windy conditions, avoid lighting fires. Use barbecues only where permitted in designated areas and follow local restrictions. Dispose of cigarettes safely and never discard hot ashes.
Follow evacuation instructions promptly. Routes can become dangerous as wind and smoke change; follow the emergency services rather than relying on a fixed escape direction.

ito-guide--water-boiling.mu.content:
>Boiling water
Use heat to deal with germs when local notices permit boiling.
Equipment: stable stove or safe permitted heat source, pot with lid, clean covered container and a timer.
1. Set up the stove outdoors on a level surface. Keep handles where they cannot be knocked and keep the clean lid away from raw water. Settle or strain cloudy water first.
2. Bring clear water to a full rolling boil. Start timing when the whole surface is churning. Continue for one minute, or three minutes above about 2,000 metres. Follow the supplier's instructions during a local boil-water notice.
3. Turn off the heat and let the batch cool covered. Pour into a clean container without dipping a raw scoop into it. Keep it separate from water waiting for treatment.
4. Restart the timer if the boil stopped before the interval finished. Use a different supply where fuel, toxic chemicals, radioactive material or flood contamination is suspected.

ito-guide--water-cold-source.mu.content:
>Water collection in freezing conditions
Plan for frozen bottles, extra fuel and longer treatment times.
1. Look for an accessible liquid source from stable ground. Keep off unverified ice and out of cold moving water. Use carried reserves or turn back if there is no safe approach.
2. If snow is the only practical source, collect clean-looking snow from an undisturbed area away from pavements, droppings or fuel. Use a little liquid water in the pot if available and add small amounts of snow as it melts. Expect low yield and significant fuel use.
3. Treat the melt for germs just like raw surface water. Boil at the applicable time or follow the chemical product's cold-water directions. Reject suspected chemical contamination.
4. Protect filled bottles and water filters from freezing. Keep some safe water immediately available and avoid making a cold, thirsty group wait while you melt an entire batch.

ito-guide--water-dehydration.mu.content:
>Recognising and managing dehydration
Start replacing fluid early while the person can drink safely.
1. Look for thirst, dry mouth, darker or reduced urine, headache and dizziness. Babies may have fewer wet nappies or no tears. Do not use urine colour by itself to diagnose severity.
2. Rest in a cool place and offer frequent small sips of safe water. For vomiting or diarrhoea, commercial oral rehydration salts can help replace water and salts. Use the exact safe-water volume printed on the packet.
3. Reassess alertness, urination and ability to keep fluids down. Persistent dizziness when standing, rapid breathing, markedly reduced urine or inability to keep fluids down warrants urgent advice.
4. Seek emergency help if the person becomes confused, difficult to wake or breathes abnormally. Do not give a drink to anyone who cannot swallow safely.

ito-guide--water-disinfection.mu.content:
>Chemical disinfection
Use a product labelled for treating drinking water and keep the instructions with it.
1. Read the package before measuring water. Check expiration, target organisms, water volume, contact time and directions for cold or cloudy water. Products and concentrations differ.
2. Settle and strain cloudy water. Measure the actual batch volume and add the labelled dose. Mix as directed and note when treatment finishes. Keep the container sealed and marked while you wait.
3. Some disinfectants have poor coverage against parasites such as Cryptosporidium. If the product cannot cover the likely organisms, boil or combine suitable filtration and disinfection following both instructions.
4. Do not improvise use of scented bleach, cleaning tablets or more concentrated doses. Do not treat chemically polluted water this way. If you cannot verify the dose, contact time or suitability, use another safe method or source.

ito-guide--water-filtration.mu.content:
>Water filters and their limits
Read the device rating before relying on a portable filter.
1. Match treatment to the risk. Many backpacking microfilters remove protozoa and some bacteria but miss viruses. For uncertain microbial risks, boil or pair a suitable filter with a compatible disinfection step. Reject sources suspected of chemical pollution.
2. Mark the inlet, scoop and raw bag. Assemble as directed and keep the outlet above and clear of the raw vessel. Settle heavily silty water first to reduce clogging.
3. Collect into a cleaned bottle and cap it. If the raw inlet touches the clean bottle mouth or outlet, treat any affected water again and clean the contaminated parts according to the instructions.
4. If flow slows, service or backflush exactly as instructed, using safe water as specified. Stop using a cracked filter or one that may have frozen when wet until the manufacturer confirms it is usable. Normal flow cannot prove membrane integrity.

ito-guide--water-private-supply.mu.content:
>Wells and boreholes after flooding
Switch to confirmed safe water if a private supply is flooded or treatment fails.

1. Stop using suspect water for drinking, food, ice, brushing teeth and infant feeds. Use sealed bottled water or another confirmed safe supply. Follow any restrictions on other uses.
2. In England and Wales, contact the council team responsible for private water supplies. Elsewhere ask the local drinking-water or public health authority. Tell them whether the wellhead flooded, nearby sewage or fuel may have spilled, or the pump or treatment lost power.
3. Ask a qualified contractor to inspect the wellhead, pump and treatment. Keep away from flooded electrical equipment. Professional cleaning or disinfection may be needed.
4. Keep using the alternative supply until testing and local advice confirm the water is safe. Clear water and a running UV lamp cannot confirm this. Boiling cannot remove fuel or other toxic chemicals.

ito-guide--water-rainwater.mu.content:
>Collecting rainwater
Treat collected rain as a separate supply with contamination risks.
1. For temporary collection, stretch a clean sheet between secure supports with one low corner draining into a clean raw-water container. Keep the collection surface off the ground, clear of smoke, droppings and damaged or dirty coatings.
2. Let the first runoff wash loose dirt away before placing the container under the corner. Cover and label it as raw rainwater. Discard foul-smelling or visibly contaminated batches.
3. Keep roof and water-butt runoff for non-drinking uses unless the supply and treatment have been assessed for drinking. Roofs and gutters can add both microbes and chemicals.
4. Keep drinking water separate. A first flush, mesh screen or ordinary boil does not remove dissolved contaminants. Use a confirmed potable supply for drinking whenever available.

ito-guide--water-ration.mu.content:
>Managing a limited water supply
Track safe water and reduce avoidable uses before the reserve runs low.
1. Write down litres on hand, when a safe resupply is expected, and who needs water. Include cooking, hygiene and medical needs. Mark each container by use and count only accessible potable water in the drinking total.
2. Set regular checks on supply and people. Use meals requiring little water and postpone washing jobs that can wait. Keep safe water for drinking, food preparation, wound care and essential hygiene.
3. Use separately labelled utility water for permitted non-potable uses. Keep its buckets and hoses away from clean equipment. Fix obvious leaks if safe.
4. Do not compensate by drinking floodwater or severely restricting safe drinking water. If the reserve cannot meet needs, seek a verified resupply or move while a safe route is available.

ito-guide--water-safe-water.mu.content:
>Making water safe
Identify the hazard and follow the supplier notice before treating water.

1. If there is a notice, read the exact wording. A boil-water notice gives instructions for using boiled water. Under a do-not-drink or do-not-use notice, use a confirmed safe alternative and follow the stated restrictions. Do not assume boiling makes it usable.
2. Use confirmed safe water for drinks, food preparation, ice, teeth and cleaning infant feeding equipment. Follow local health advice for preparing infant feeds.
3. If there is no safe supply or applicable notice, and the concern is germs only, settle or strain cloudy water first. Bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above about 2,000 m. Let it cool, covered, and pour it from a clean container.
4. If you cannot boil, follow drinking-water treatment instructions exactly. Check which organisms the product covers. A cloth removes sediment. An ordinary portable filter can miss viruses, and some disinfectants do not reliably kill parasites.
5. Reject floodwater and sources suspected to contain fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material. Boiling and routine portable treatment cannot make them safe.

ito-guide--water-settling.mu.content:
>Settling and straining raw water
Remove suspended dirt before treating water for germs.
Equipment: two marked raw-water containers and a clean tightly woven cloth or coffee filter.
1. Let muddy water stand undisturbed until heavier particles sink. Slowly decant the clearer upper layer into a second container. Stop before the sediment moves.
2. Stretch the cloth or paper across the receiving container and pour gradually. Swap it when blocked. Keep the strained batch on the raw side of your setup.
3. Boil or apply a suitable treatment with the required contact time. A cloth, gravel or improvised charcoal strainer cannot make water potable. It can leave pathogens and dissolved contaminants behind.
4. If clarity does not improve, switch sources if possible. Disinfection and UV products can be less effective in cloudy water. Follow the device or product instructions rather than shortening contact time.

ito-guide--water-sources.mu.content:
>Finding emergency water
Work from known potable supplies towards sources that need treatment.
1. Check sealed bottles, home reserves and confirmed distribution points first. If using a map, mark several potential sources and routes that avoid steep banks and crossings. A mapped stream may be dry, especially in summer.
2. Evaluate a source from the bank. Check upstream for farms, sewage outlets, industrial sites, heavy road runoff, mining, algae, fuel sheen or floodwater. Move to a different supply if you suspect chemical contamination. Clear water and fast flow are no evidence of safety.
3. Prefer an accessible source with a safe approach and water you can collect without wading. Treat water from springs, streams and lakes as potentially contaminated by germs. Return before darkness or rising water cuts off your route.
4. If collecting for a group, carry marked raw and clean containers. Record where the water came from so you can stop using a suspect source.

ito-guide--water-storage.mu.content:
>Storing drinking water
Build a reserve before you need it and keep it separate from utility water.

1. As a planning baseline, aim for about 4 litres per person per day for three days for drinking, food preparation and basic hygiene. Two people need about 24 litres for that period. Allow extra for heat, illness, pregnancy, pets and any medical needs.
2. Keep sealed bottled water or fill clean, sanitised food-grade containers from a confirmed safe supply. Choose tight lids and sizes you can lift when full. Never reuse a container that held fuel, pesticides or other toxic chemicals.
3. Mark home-filled containers with the fill date and replace the water every six months. For commercial bottles, follow the label. Store them somewhere cool, away from sunlight and chemicals. Where flooding is possible, store them above likely flood level.
4. Pour or use a clean tap rather than dipping hands or cups into the reserve. Clearly label and separately store anything intended only for flushing or washing.

ito-guide--water-surface.mu.content:
>Collecting water from streams and lakes
Carry a raw-water scoop, a marked raw container and a separate clean bottle.
1. Pick a firm, low bank. Avoid floodwater, rapid flow, unstable edges and suspected chemical pollution or algal blooms. Leave if your only approach requires wading or leaning over a drop.
2. Take water from below surface debris and above bottom sediment. Use the scoop from stable ground and pour into the raw container. Avoid stirring up the bed with your feet or container.
3. Seal and mark raw water. Keep the scoop and the wet outside of its container clear of cleaned bottle mouths, filter outlets and cooking utensils.
4. If turbid, settle or strain before treatment. Boil for microbial risks where possible. A filter and disinfectant may be needed together if boiling is unavailable. Carry untreated water separately until you get back to a safe treatment site.
